item.title: The Back Office with Vinay
item.description: In 2012, before we had a tech team, our second tech vendor was KuVi, a services company Vinay Kumar C started right after college. Vinay was introduced to us by Renuka, who’s now an AVP on our support team. She said she had a friend who could take care of all our tech needs, from hosting our website to building our first CRM and pretty much everything else. We said yes, partly because they were charging us just ₹15,000 a month.

item.title: Jio Platforms and a record day for delivery selling
item.description: Yesterday was probably a record day for equity delivery selling, thanks to Jio Platforms, with investors selling shares after the listing. By the way, our customers would have saved anywhere between ₹1.5 crore and ₹10 crore in brokerage alone, based on what others charge. This doesn’t include potential additional savings on DP charges, ours is one of the lowest. Our brokerage on equity delivery is still zero.🙂

item.title: Unintended consequences of higher STT and F&O curbs
item.description: Across Zerodha, here’s roughly the percentage of individual traders who are profitable: Futures: ≈50% Option sellers: ≈40% Option buyers: ≈10% MTF: too early to tell, considering it’s a new product One of the unintended consequences of increasing STT and all the other measures to curb F&O speculation is that they may have pushed traders toward even riskier trading behaviour. Yes, in theory, losses from buying options are limited to the premium paid.

item.title: What are you using Kite APIs for?
item.description: Now that Kite APIs are free, how are you using them with AI agents? What have you built? AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex have made it much easier for traders and investors to build their own tools, even without much coding experience. We’re also seeing more people use Kite APIs because of these coding agents.

item.title: Intermission by The Ken - the story of TCS
item.description: History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. With everything happening around AI, it feels like we’ve seen versions of this story before. Technologies change, industries get disrupted, and businesses that once seemed permanent disappear. The latest episode of Intermission by The Ken is on TCS, and one thing stood out to me. In the 1960s, India had only a few dozen computers, and even that was enough for unions to protest, fearing they would take away jobs.

item.title: History may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes
item.description: In a world where growth and revenues are almost always prioritised over risk, I think it helps to look back at history and remind ourselves of the follies of humankind. After all, history may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes. I just finished reading 1873 by Liaquat Ahamed, about the Vienna stock market crash that eventually triggered a global financial crisis. I had read 1929 by Andrew Ross Sorkin last year, which explores a similar theme.

item.title: Rainmatter Originals - Turning wastewater into a resource
item.description: Recently, I wrote about how serious our water problem is getting. This year’s weak monsoon has made it worse, and in Bengaluru, for example, that means dry borewells and expensive tankers. But we’re also wasting water we’ve already cleaned. Large apartments have to treat their own sewage, but only 20–30% of that water gets used. The rest goes down the drain. Meanwhile, IT parks and factories a few kilometers away are buying tanker water for their cooling towers.

item.title: Why NPS works well for long-term retirement investing
item.description: When you’re in your 20s or 30s, retirement is probably the last thing on your mind. But that’s also when you have the biggest advantage when it comes to investing: time. The challenge, however, isn’t just starting early. It’s staying invested for decades without dipping into your retirement savings along the way. One of the most underrated aspects of retirement investing is having money that’s not easily accessible. This forced discipline can make a huge difference over the long term.

item.title: The other side of MTF growth
item.description: Most of the growth in the industry’s MTF book is in small and microcaps. These are the stocks where liquidity tends to dry up first when markets either fall or go sideways, like they are right now😬

item.title: IPOs are the only bullish corner of the market right now
item.description: The only bullish corner of the market right now is IPOs. The broader market has been steadily falling. The numbers may not fully show it, but it certainly feels like a bear market. IPOs, on the other hand, are a full-on party. Most recent listings have done well, and you can see it in the rush of activity. I don’t remember the last time we saw such a stark divergence between the primary and secondary markets.

item.title: It’s never too early to start investing
item.description: Our youngest customer is just 28 days old. The parents opened a Zerodha minor account, and a week later, they made the first investment.

item.title: The Back Office with Shoaib
item.description: One lesser-known thing about Zerodha is that almost everyone in leadership today has grown from within the organisation. We have rarely hired anyone from outside for leadership roles. For most people here, Zerodha was their first or second job, and we don’t really have anyone with a pedigree education either. Shoaib is a good example. He started as a support agent, went on to head account opening, and eventually became our head of HR.

item.title: Solving India’s water crisis starts with knowing the problem
item.description: Water is probably the thing we take most for granted, and it is going to become one of the defining issues of our times. As climate change worsens, we are going to see more erratic monsoon patterns, and that will only exacerbate an already difficult problem. A lot of India is already under water stress. In places like Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, we are simply extracting more groundwater every year than is being replenished.

item.title: Regulation can change the economics of a business overnight
item.description: I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today’s IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is a good reminder. Broking is no different. A change in rules around retail F&O trading, how brokers can earn on client float, MTF requirements, or any of several other areas can change the economics of the business almost overnight. So when valuing regulated businesses, you can’t just extrapolate current revenues and profits into the future.

item.title: Coming soon Nudge v2
item.description: Coming soon: Nudge v2 will do more than just warnings, allowing you to set hard limits to stay disciplined.

item.title: Opening an account is easy, closing it should be too
item.description: People need to be able to close an account as easily as they open one, if not easier. Making it easy to open an account but impossible to close one is the oldest dark pattern in the book. I think we are one of the few apps where the account closure option is clearly visible. We at Zerodha close around 15,000 to 20,000 accounts every month for reasons ranging from company policies and trading losses to moving to another broker.

item.title: Thoughts on MDR for UPI transactions
item.description: I think MDR on UPI was probably inevitable at some point, especially given how widespread UPI adoption has become. It could also lead to more competition, instead of just three apps accounting for more than 95% of the market. That being said, there are some use cases, like investing and broking, where the proposed MDR structure doesn’t really make sense. The problem with broking is that there is no guarantee that money transferred to a broker will actually result in a transaction.

item.title: In finance, boring is usually better
item.description: The fancier a financial product looks, the bigger the catch usually is. Prateek Singh and Zero1 do a nice job explaining this using leasing vs buying a car. A lower monthly payment can make leasing look like an obvious deal, but once you account for upfront costs, restrictions, and what you actually own at the end, the math looks very different. I think this is true for most financial products. If it takes more than two sentences to explain how a product makes money and where the risk sits, you should probably stay away.

item.title: Rainmatter Originals - The story of Hasiru Dala Innovations and Carbon Masters
item.description: Bangalore produces around 7,000 tonnes of waste a day, roughly 3,000 tonnes of that is wet waste. All of it has to be collected, segregated, and processed every single day. A lot of it still ends up badly treated or in a landfill. We got to know the Hasiru Dala Innovations team a few years ago. They’ve spent years doing the thankless part of this, collecting and segregating waste at scale.

item.title: The role NSE played in Zerodha’s early days
item.description: Back in 2010, one of the reasons we even considered becoming a brokerage firm was because of NSE NOW. It was a free trading platform provided by the NSE that brokers could offer to their clients. While we were starting out, I had heard a lot of scary stories about the exchanges, but our experience was the total opposite. When we went to Chennai to inquire about a membership, they were incredibly welcoming.
